summary: Specifies the base protocol for Routing Bridges, which forward at layer 2 without configuration while supporting multipath and staying safe during temporary loops. They use IS-IS routing and a header with a hop count, and remain compatible with existing IEEE 802.1 bridges.

plainLanguage.summary: Ordinary Ethernet switches avoid loops by blocking ports, so traffic is forced onto a few links. RBridges apply link-state routing at Layer 2: they map the network with IS-IS, use many paths at once, and count hops so a temporary loop cannot run forever, while computers and IP routers still see plain Ethernet.

subtitle: Ethernet switches that route with IS-IS and a hop count: shortest paths, multipathing, and no spanning tree.

tldr.problem: Spanning-tree bridges block redundant links, so traffic piles onto a few links and takes non-shortest paths. Ethernet frames also have no hop count, which makes temporary loops dangerous.
tldr.mechanism: RBridges run the IS-IS link-state protocol among themselves, wrap each frame in a TRILL header that carries a hop count and 16-bit ingress and egress nicknames, and unwrap it at the last RBridge. Multicast and unknown-destination frames travel on shared distribution trees.
tldr.outcome: The result is shortest-path, multipath forwarding with no required configuration that can replace customer bridges step by step. The RFC is a Proposed Standard-track base specification that many later RFCs update.

today: RFC 6325 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by many later RFCs, including RFC 6327, RFC 6439 and RFC 8139. Read those with it for the complete current specification.

sections.title: Why Routing Bridges
sections.content:
IP subnets need per-port configuration, while IEEE 802.1 bridges glue many links into what looks like one LAN. But spanning-tree bridging has costs: it blocks ports, so traffic is concentrated on selected links; forwarding follows whatever path the tree leaves rather than the shortest one; the Ethernet header has no hop count, which is dangerous during temporary loops; and VLANs can partition when the tree reconfigures.

The RFC presents RBridges (Routing Bridges), which implement the TRILL protocol, as the application of link-state routing to VLAN-aware customer bridging. With the exceptions the document lists, RBridges can incrementally replace 802.1Q-2005 or 802.1D customer bridges. The specification focuses on IEEE 802.3 links and is meant for LAN scale, not for scaling beyond existing bridged LANs.

The text also contains a short poem, the Algorhyme V2 by Ray Perlner, that summarizes the idea: least-cost paths, hop counts so that the network need not be loop-free, and no common spanning tree.
sections.plainLanguage: Traditional Ethernet switches avoid loops by blocking ports, so traffic uses few links and takes whatever path remains. RBridges run a routing protocol among themselves instead, so every link stays in use, each frame follows a least-cost path, and a hop count in the header limits damage if a temporary loop appears.

sections.title: How RBridges Fit Together
sections.content:
RBridges run a link-state protocol among themselves, which lets them compute pair-wise optimal paths for unicast and distribution trees for frames going to unknown or multicast destinations. The first RBridge a frame meets, the ingress RBridge, encapsulates it with a TRILL header naming the last RBridge, the egress RBridge, where it is decapsulated.

A frame on an Ethernet link has an outer Ethernet header, the TRILL header, the original inner Ethernet header, the payload and the FCS. The outer header changes at every hop, with the next-hop RBridge as destination and the transmitting RBridge as source, while the inner frame, including its VLAN tag, is preserved. Because transit RBridges forward on the egress RBridge, their unicast tables are sized by the number of RBridges, not end nodes.

On each link the RBridges elect one Designated RBridge (DRB). It picks the Designated VLAN used between RBridges and appoints, per VLAN, which RBridge on the link is the appointed forwarder that encapsulates and decapsulates the link's traffic. At most one RBridge may do so for a given VLAN at any time.

RBridges do not run spanning tree or block ports. Bridges not yet replaced are transparent to RBridge traffic and appear as multi-access links, so a campus can be upgraded gradually. RBridges here supply customer services only, not provider bridging.
sections.plainLanguage: The first RBridge a frame meets adds a TRILL header that names the last RBridge. Each RBridge on the path replaces only the outer Ethernet header and lowers the hop count; the original frame is left unchanged. On each shared link, one RBridge is elected to handle the link's traffic for each VLAN, which keeps the network free of loops at the entry and exit points.

sections.title: The TRILL Header
sections.content:
The TRILL header begins with a 2-bit Version (zero in this document; an RBridge MUST silently discard a frame with a version it does not recognize), two reserved bits that MUST be zero when added, a 1-bit M flag, a 5-bit Op-Length and a 6-bit Hop Count. Then come the 16-bit egress and ingress RBridge nicknames, followed by any options.

When M = 0, the egress nickname is the egress RBridge of a known unicast address. When M = 1, it names the distribution tree to use. Neither nickname may be changed by transit RBridges. An RBridge drops a frame whose hop count is zero and otherwise decrements it. The ingress RBridge SHOULD set the unicast hop count above the number of hops it expects, to allow for alternate routing.

Op-Length counts the options in 4-octet units, up to 124 octets. If the CHbH (critical hop-by-hop) bit is set, a transit RBridge that does not support all critical options MUST drop the frame; if the CItE (critical ingress-to-egress) bit is set, an unsupporting egress RBridge MUST drop it. Frames with options may take a slower path.
sections.plainLanguage: The header holds a 6-bit hop count, the 16-bit nickname of the RBridge where the frame leaves the TRILL network, and the 16-bit nickname of the RBridge that added the header. One flag says whether the second nickname names a destination RBridge or a distribution tree. A frame at hop count zero is discarded.

sections.title: IS-IS Routing and Nicknames
sections.content:
TRILL uses an extension of IS-IS as its routing protocol. IS-IS runs directly over Layer 2, so it works without assigning IP addresses, and it is easy to extend with new TLV data elements. TRILL runs its own IS-IS instance, separate from any Layer 3 one, in a single Level 1 area with fixed area address zero. TRILL IS-IS frames use the L2-IS-IS Ethertype, have no TRILL header and are never forwarded.

Each RBridge has a 48-bit IS-IS System ID, usually derived from one of its MAC addresses. A nickname is a 16-bit abbreviation of that identity, picked dynamically and piggybacked on IS-IS. Values 0x0000 and 0xFFC0 to 0xFFFF cannot be chosen. Each RBridge picks randomly from apparently free values, and if two choose the same one, the one with the numerically higher priority or System ID keeps it and the other must choose again. An RBridge may be configured with a nickname, which gives it priority.

The DRB election uses TRILL-Hello messages, a variant of the Layer 3 IS-IS LAN Hello. The DRB is chosen solely on priority and MAC address, because with several DRBs on a Layer 2 link loops could form. Hellos are not padded. RBridges also test link sizes with optional MTU-probe and MTU-ack messages; the default and minimum campus size Sz is 1470 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The RBridges exchange IS-IS link-state messages, so each one can compute the same map of the campus. Each RBridge also picks a 16-bit nickname, a short name for itself that goes in TRILL headers. If two RBridges pick the same value, one of them keeps it and the other picks again.

sections.title: Distribution Trees for Multi-Destination Traffic
sections.content:
Multi-destination frames are unicast frames with an unknown destination, multicast frames and broadcast frames. They travel along distribution trees, which reach every RBridge, are shared across all VLANs and are pruned per VLAN and for IP multicast so frames go only where they might be wanted. Trees are not spanning trees. Each RBridge computes them from the link-state database with a shortest-path-first run from the chosen root, and no extra messages are needed.

When several equal-cost parents exist, tree number j picks parent j mod p from the parents ordered by IS-IS ID, so different trees use different links. The RBridge whose nickname has the highest tree-root priority (default 0x8000) says how many trees the campus computes, which defaults to one.

Four checks guard against loops: the tree adjacency check, the RPF check (reverse path forwarding, that the frame arrives from the expected link for its ingress and tree), the parallel links check and the port group check. A frame failing the first two MUST be dropped. On a topology change an RBridge MUST adjust its input filters no later than its output forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: Frames that must reach many destinations follow a tree of paths computed from the same map. The trees are pruned per VLAN and for IP multicast so a frame is not copied onto links that cannot use it. Four tests at each RBridge reject copies that arrive from an unexpected direction, which stops loops while the network is changing.

sections.title: Handling Frames
sections.content:
The RFC sorts Layer 2 frames into five categories: Layer 2 control frames (such as BPDUs), native frames, TRILL Data frames (Ethertype 0x22F3), TRILL control frames (Ethertype 0x22F4, L2-IS-IS) and TRILL other frames, which conformant RBridges MUST discard. RBridges MUST NOT encapsulate or forward BPDUs.

For a native unicast frame, the ingress RBridge looks up the VLAN and destination. If the egress RBridge is known, it encapsulates with M = 0, the next hop as outer destination, and sends it on. If the destination is unknown, it treats the frame like a broadcast. Native multicast and broadcast frames go out with M = 1 and the All-RBridges outer address, down a chosen tree, and in native form on its other links where it is appointed forwarder.

For a received TRILL frame, a sequence of tests applies: wrong version, zero hop count, mismatched unicast and M bit, or no IS-IS adjacency with the neighbor lead to discard. A transit RBridge decrements the hop count and forwards. An egress RBridge learns the inner source address against the ingress nickname, decapsulates and sends the native frame onto the right link. An inhibited appointed forwarder discards native frames in that VLAN for a time of zero to 30 seconds, default 30, after it sees a spanning tree root bridge change.
sections.plainLanguage: An RBridge first sorts each arriving frame by type. Ordinary frames from local computers are encapsulated and sent toward their egress RBridge, or down a distribution tree if their destination is unknown. TRILL frames that arrive are checked, then either forwarded with a lower hop count or, at the last RBridge, unwrapped and delivered.

sections.title: Learning End-Station Addresses
sections.content:
RBridges learn which RBridge each end-station MAC address and VLAN sits behind. There are five ways: watching VLAN frames on ports where it is the appointed forwarder, noting the ingress nickname of frames it decapsulates, Layer 2 registration protocols, the optional ESADI protocol, and management configuration. RBridges MUST implement the first two and SHOULD implement configuration.

Each learned entry has a one-octet confidence level. Entries learned from observing data default to 0x20, ESADI information carries 0 to 254, and manual entries default to 255. A new entry with equal or higher confidence replaces an older one, which in the default case mimics ordinary 802.1 bridge learning. Higher confidence for authenticated sources can resist forged frames.

Entries age out. The default Ageing Time is 300 seconds, configurable from 10 to 1,000,000 seconds. When an RBridge loses appointed forwarder status for a VLAN, it forgets the addresses it learned there, and other RBridges shorten their aging for entries from it to at most the Forward Delay (default 15 seconds, range 4 to 30).
sections.plainLanguage: An RBridge builds a table that maps each computer's MAC address and VLAN to the RBridge that leads to it. It learns this table by watching traffic, and it can also accept registered or manually configured entries that are trusted more highly than observed traffic. Old entries are deleted after a few minutes so a computer that moves is found again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says Layer 2 bridging is not inherently secure, for example it is subject to spoofing of source addresses and bridging control messages, and the goal is that RBridges add no new issues beyond those. Countermeasures include IS-IS security for TRILL IS-IS and ESADI (which then needs configuration) and IEEE 802.1X and 802.1AE below TRILL. RBridges do not stop impersonation such as bogus ARP or ND replies.

Because frames are encapsulated in transit, TRILL-ignorant firewall devices that RBridges cannot detect as end stations may be unable to inspect them. VLANs give logical separation only if all RBridges and links are secured and end stations cannot use dynamic VLAN registration. Replacing bridges with RBridges can also send data along the least-cost path regardless of VLAN, so end-to-end encryption is suggested.

Forged BPDUs or forged TRILL-Hello frames claiming appointed forwarder status could falsely inhibit forwarding. The best defense is IS-IS security. In an all-RBridge point-to-point campus, a forger mostly denies service to itself, but bridged LANs, which look like multi-access links, are more exposed.
sections.plainLanguage: RBridges add no new security problems beyond ordinary Ethernet switches, and they do not fix the old ones. Signed IS-IS messages can protect the control traffic. Because frames are wrapped while in transit, firewalls that inspect Ethernet frames directly may not see the original content, so encrypting the data end to end is advised.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Reserved; set to zero by the ingress RBridge.

fields.name: M
fields.desc: 1 means the egress nickname names a distribution tree.

fields.name: Op-Length
fields.desc: Length of the options in 4-octet units.

fields.name: Hop Count
fields.desc: Decremented at each RBridge; dropped at zero.

fields.name: Egress RBridge Nickname
fields.desc: Egress RBridge, or the tree when M is 1.
